And several groups, notably Mark Stokes and Earl Miller's laboratories from around 2013, have shown that information can be decoded from an 'activity-silent' state, apparently carried by short-term changes in synaptic weights that can be read out by a pulse of input, without any elevated firing. A third family of theories emphasises rhythms. On the account developed by Ole Jensen, Earl Miller and others, items are held in distinct phases of an ongoing slow theta oscillation of roughly 4 to 8 hertz, each item expressed as a burst of faster gamma activity of 30 hertz and above riding on its own phase. The capacity limit then falls out of arithmetic: the number of gamma cycles that fit inside one theta cycle is about four to seven. This is an elegant explanation of why the number is small and roughly constant, and there is supportive evidence from human electrophysiology, but it remains a hypothesis rather than an established fact. Neuromodulation adds another layer. Dopamine acting at D1 receptors in prefrontal cortex has an inverted-U relationship with performance, so both too little and too much impair it, which is one reason stimulant medication helps some people and degrades others, and why acute stress, which floods the prefrontal cortex with catecholamines, characteristically causes the mind to go blank.

sections.heading: Differences Between People and Across a Lifetime
sections.body: Working memory capacity differs substantially between individuals, and those differences predict a great deal. Complex span scores correlate with fluid intelligence, the ability to solve novel problems, at a level high enough that some researchers have argued the two constructs are nearly identical at the latent level, though the consensus is now that they are strongly related but distinct. Span predicts reading comprehension, the acquisition of a second language, mathematical achievement, following multi-step instructions, and performance in complex real-world jobs such as air traffic control. Randall Engle and colleagues have argued persuasively that the active ingredient is not storage as such but attention control: the ability to keep a goal active and to resist interference from what is salient but irrelevant. High-span individuals are better at the antisaccade task, where you must look away from a suddenly appearing target, and are less likely to notice their own name in an unattended channel, which is exactly what you would predict if their advantage is in shielding rather than in raw storage. Development follows a slow rise and a slow fall. Immediate span in a four-year-old is around two items; by seven it is around four; adult levels of roughly six or seven digits are reached in the mid-teens, and complex span continues improving into the early twenties as executive control matures alongside the protracted development of prefrontal cortex. Part of the childhood improvement is genuine capacity growth and part is strategy: cumulative rehearsal appears spontaneously around age seven, and before that children simply do not repeat items to themselves. Decline begins gradually from the twenties or thirties on some measures, accelerates after sixty, and is much steeper for tasks requiring manipulation and interference resolution than for simple storage. An eighty-year-old often has a nearly normal digit span and a substantially reduced backward digit span or operation span, which is a useful clinical distinction. Clinically, reduced working memory is a feature of many conditions rather than a diagnosis in itself. It is prominent in ADHD, where it is entangled with attention control; in developmental language disorder and dyslexia, where phonological loop function is often specifically weak; in schizophrenia, where it is one of the most reliable cognitive findings; and after traumatic brain injury or stroke affecting frontoparietal networks. Heritability estimates from twin studies run around 40 to 60 per cent in adults, but the honest reading of that figure is that it describes variation in a particular population under particular conditions and says nothing about the malleability of any individual. Sleep loss, acute stress, pain, anxiety, hunger, and the early stages of many illnesses all depress measured capacity temporarily, sometimes by an amount comparable to decades of aging, which is worth remembering before drawing conclusions from a single bad test.

sections.heading: Cognitive Load Theory: The Bridge to Teaching
sections.body: The most productive application of working memory research to practice is cognitive load theory, developed by the Australian educational psychologist John Sweller from the 1980s onward. Its founding premise is stark: because working memory is tiny and long-term memory is vast, the entire purpose of instruction is to build organised knowledge in long-term memory, and any instructional design that overloads the workspace prevents that from happening. Learning is not something that happens in working memory; it is something that has to survive passage through it. Sweller distinguished three sources of load. Intrinsic load is the inherent difficulty of the material, determined by element interactivity, the number of items that must be held simultaneously because they can only be understood in relation to each other. Learning the chemical symbols for twenty elements is low in element interactivity, since each can be learned alone; balancing an equation is high, because the terms constrain one another. Extraneous load is imposed by the way material is presented rather than by the material itself, and is pure waste. Germane load is the effort devoted to building schemas, though in later formulations Sweller folded this into intrinsic load rather than treating it as a third pool. Several robust design effects follow. The worked example effect, demonstrated repeatedly since Sweller and Graham Cooper's 1985 algebra studies, is that novices learn more from studying fully worked solutions than from solving equivalent problems themselves, because unguided problem solving forces means-ends analysis that consumes the whole workspace on search while leaving nothing for noticing structure. The split-attention effect is that a diagram with a separate legend, or text on one page referring to a figure on another, forces the learner to hold one source in memory while searching the other; integrating labels into the diagram removes the cost. The redundancy effect is that presenting the same information in two forms simultaneously, such as reading aloud text that is also on screen, harms learning, because the learner cannot help reconciling them. The modality effect is that a diagram with spoken rather than written explanation uses both the visual and verbal subsystems and therefore has a larger effective capacity. The most important qualification is the expertise reversal effect, documented by Slava Kalyuga and colleagues from around 1998. Every one of these guidelines reverses as expertise grows. Worked examples that help novices actively hinder more advanced learners, who learn more from solving; integrated explanations that support a beginner become redundant clutter for someone who already knows the material. There is no instructional design that is optimal for all learners, only designs matched to a level of prior knowledge. That is uncomfortable for anyone hoping for a universal method, and it is the single finding most often ignored when the theory is applied carelessly.

sections.heading: Working Memory in Reading, Arithmetic and Conversation
sections.body: The limits become visible in ordinary competences once you look for them. Reading is the clearest case. To understand a sentence you must hold its earlier parts until later parts arrive to resolve them, and English permits structures that stretch this badly. A centre-embedded sentence such as 'the rat the cat the dog chased killed ate the malt' is perfectly grammatical and essentially unparsable, because it requires holding three unresolved noun phrases before any verb arrives. One level of embedding is easy, two is hard, three defeats almost everyone, and that ceiling maps neatly onto the capacity estimates. Garden-path sentences such as 'the horse raced past the barn fell' fail for a related reason: the initial parse must be discarded and rebuilt, and the raw material for rebuilding has already begun to decay. Good prose style, in the sense that Joseph Williams and others have taught it, is largely a set of techniques for reducing the distance over which a reader must hold something unresolved: keep subject and verb close, put the familiar information first, break long conditional chains into separate sentences. Arithmetic shows the limit in an even more measurable way. Multiplying two two-digit numbers mentally requires holding the operands, generating partial products, holding those, and adding them, all while the earlier contents decay. Most adults fail on 47 times 68 not because they cannot execute any step but because a partial result evaporates while another is being computed. Children with weak working memory show a characteristic pattern in class: they lose their place in multi-step procedures, abandon tasks partway through, and fail to follow instructions of the form 'put your books away, take out your reading folder, and line up by the door', which contains three chunks plus the context of what one is meant to be doing. Susan Gathercole and Tracy Alloway's classroom research found that such children are frequently described by teachers as inattentive or unmotivated, which is close to the opposite of the truth. Conversation and listening carry the same tax. Simultaneous interpreters, who must hold an incoming clause while producing the previous one, work in short shifts of twenty to thirty minutes for exactly this reason. Following a spoken direction such as 'take the second left after the church, then right at the roundabout, then it is the third house on the left past the postbox' presents four or five chunks in sequence with no chance to re-read, and the ordinary failure to retain it is not inattention. In every one of these cases the fix is the same in principle: reduce the number of things that must be held at once, or shift some of them out of the head and onto paper, a screen, a diagram or a repeated confirmation.

sections.heading: Failure Modes: Overload, Interruption, Stress and Sleep
sections.body: Working memory does not fail gracefully or announce itself. Its failures present as other things, which is why they are so often misattributed to character. Overload is the simplest mode. Beyond capacity, performance does not degrade evenly; items are lost, usually the middle ones, and the person is frequently unaware of the loss. Confidence is a poor guide to whether something was held. Worse, when overloaded, people fall back on simpler strategies without noticing, substituting a heuristic for the computation they intended, which produces answers that feel reasoned but are not. Interruption is the most expensive and the most underestimated. When a task is interrupted, the goal state and the intermediate results in the workspace are lost, and the cost of resumption is not the length of the interruption but the effort of rebuilding. Gloria Mark's field studies of office workers found average resumption lags in the range of twenty minutes for a substantive interrupted task, and controlled laboratory studies find that interruptions of only a few seconds roughly double error rates on sequential procedures. Erik Altmann and Gregory Trafton's memory-for-goals work showed that even a 2.8-second interruption doubled sequence errors, and a 4.4-second one tripled them. This is the mechanism behind the disproportionate danger of interrupting a pilot on a checklist, a nurse drawing up a dose, or a surgeon counting instruments, and behind the post-completion error, where the last step of a procedure, the one after the main goal is met, is omitted: leaving the original in the photocopier, the card in the machine, the cap off the fuel tank. Acute stress attacks the system directly. Catecholamine release under stress impairs prefrontal function while strengthening more habitual striatal and amygdala-driven responses, which is why a person under threat reverts to well-drilled behaviour and cannot think flexibly. This is adaptive in a genuine emergency and disastrous in a novel one. Anxiety is subtly different: Michael Eysenck's attentional control theory holds that worry itself occupies the workspace, so an anxious person may achieve normal accuracy but only by expending far more effort, a state that looks fine on a test and is exhausting to inhabit. Sleep deprivation reduces measured capacity and, more insidiously, reduces the ability to notice the reduction. Twenty-four hours awake produces impairments on some cognitive measures comparable to a blood alcohol concentration around 0.10 per cent, above the legal driving limit in most jurisdictions, and alcohol itself impairs working memory at concentrations well below obvious intoxication. Age, illness, pain, dehydration, hypoglycaemia and hypoxia all take their toll. The common thread is that the person experiencing the reduction is a poor judge of it, so the countermeasures must be structural rather than based on self-assessment.

sections.heading: Can It Be Trained? A Cautionary Tale
sections.body: The question of whether working memory capacity can be increased by practice is the most commercially charged in the field and a genuinely instructive case in how evidence gets tested. The optimistic phase began around 2002 with Torkel Klingberg's work on adaptive training in children with ADHD, and gathered enormous momentum in 2008 when Susanne Jaeggi, Martin Buschkuehl and colleagues reported in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences that training on a demanding dual n-back task improved fluid intelligence in a dose-dependent way. If true, this would be extraordinary: a brief, cheap intervention raising the most general of cognitive abilities. A commercial industry grew rapidly around the claim. The subsequent decade largely dismantled it, and the reasons are worth understanding because they recur everywhere. Near transfer is real and uncontroversial: people who practise n-back get much better at n-back, and reasonably better at closely similar tasks. Far transfer, improvement in untrained abilities such as fluid intelligence, reading comprehension or school attainment, has consistently failed to replicate when studies used active control groups doing something equally engaging rather than passive controls doing nothing. Meta-analyses by Monica Melby-Lervag and Charles Hulme in 2013 and 2016, covering scores of studies, found reliable short-term gains on tasks resembling the trained one and essentially no durable far transfer. Randomised trials with active controls, notably a large 2013 study by Thomas Redick and colleagues, found no gains on any of seventeen transfer measures. In 2014 a consensus statement signed by around seventy cognitive scientists concluded that the marketing claims of the brain-training industry outran the evidence; the United States Federal Trade Commission fined Lumos Labs two million dollars in 2016 over deceptive advertising for Lumosity. The theoretical explanation is the one already visible in the Ericsson digit-span case. Training builds task-specific strategies and chunking structures in long-term memory rather than expanding the workspace. The runner who reached seventy-nine digits had a letter span of six. Growth in a score is not growth in a capacity. Some caution is warranted in both directions. Certain populations, particularly children with ADHD or people recovering from brain injury, do show clinically meaningful improvements on some real-world measures, though often these are rated by unblinded parents or teachers and shrink sharply under blinded assessment by someone who does not know which group the child was in. Aerobic exercise, adequate sleep and treatment of depression or anxiety have better evidence for improving cognitive performance than any commercial training program. The honest summary is that you can become far more capable in a domain by learning that domain deeply, that you can protect the capacity you have by managing sleep, stress and interruption, and that you cannot buy a bigger workspace.

sections.heading: Working With the Limit: Practical Countermeasures
sections.body: If the aperture cannot be widened, the remaining strategy is to send less through it and to build external structures that hold what the head cannot. This is not a compromise; it is how every complex human enterprise actually works, from surgical checklists to double-entry bookkeeping. The first principle is offloading. Anything written down, drawn, or laid out in physical space is no longer consuming capacity. This is why a scratch pad transforms mental arithmetic, why an outline transforms writing, why laying out ingredients before cooking prevents omissions, and why chess players calculate better with a board than blindfold. Research on cognitive offloading by Evan Risko and Sam Gilbert shows that people offload more when their internal capacity is lower or their confidence in it is lower, and that offloading genuinely improves accuracy rather than merely feeling easier. Making the environment carry information, what Donald Norman called knowledge in the world as opposed to knowledge in the head, is the most reliable single intervention available. The second is reducing what has to be held at once. When explaining, present one idea at a time and let each resolve before the next begins. Keep related information physically together so no one has to hold a legend while looking at a chart. Avoid long chains of pronouns and references. Convert a set of parallel comparisons into a table so they can be seen rather than remembered. In procedures, write the steps down and mark them off, because the specific failure mode of a remembered procedure is losing your place. The third is automation through practice. Anything practised until it runs without attention stops competing for the workspace. This is the real justification for fluency practice in arithmetic facts, letter-sound correspondences, common vocabulary and standard procedures: not that recall is intrinsically valuable but that a learner still decoding words has nothing left over for comprehension, and one still computing 7 times 8 has nothing left for the algebra it sits inside. The fourth is protecting the state you have built. Treat interruption as a hazard rather than a courtesy. Before an unavoidable interruption, write down where you are, even four words, since the cost of resumption is almost entirely the cost of reconstruction. Batch notifications. Use sterile-cockpit conventions during critical steps. Design procedures so that the last action after the main goal is achieved is impossible to omit, by making the machine keep the card until the money is taken. The fifth is respecting the physiological floor. Sleep, food, hydration and the management of pain and anxiety are not soft factors; they move measured capacity by amounts comparable to years of aging. When a task genuinely exceeds what can be held, the right response is never to try harder. It is to write it down, break it into pieces that fit, or build the knowledge that makes the pieces bigger.
